h1: Pricing beer and food combos without giving margin away
title: Pricing Beer and Food Combos for Margin | Craft Beer School
desc: How to price beer and food combos at a brewpub: margin per item, where the discount should come from and combos that move stock.
teaser: A combo should earn more per table than two separate orders. Many earn less.
standfirst: Beer and food combos are on almost every Indian brewpub menu. Built well, they lift spend per head and shift slow dishes. Built lazily, they hand back the margin your beer earns. Here is the arithmetic.
sections: Know the margin on each item first

Beer and food carry very different margins. A brewpub pint might cost ₹50 to ₹70 to make including losses and sell for ₹350 or more. A plate of food often carries a much higher cost share once you count ingredients, wastage and kitchen labour. Our guide to brewpub food menus and margins covers how to cost a dish.

Put both items of any proposed combo side by side. Here is one:

  • Wheat beer, 400 ml, ₹340. Cost ₹55. Margin ₹285.
  • Chicken tikka, ₹420. Cost ₹150. Margin ₹270.
  • Bought separately: ₹760, margin ₹555.
A combo discount has to buy something

Price that combo at ₹649 and your margin drops to ₹444. You have given away ₹111 per combo. That is fine only if it buys something you would not have had otherwise: a second round, a dish from someone who would have ordered beer alone, or a table on a slow Tuesday that would otherwise be empty.

The test is simple. For each combo sold, would the guest have bought both items anyway? If most would, the combo is a discount on existing spend. If most would have bought only one, it is a good trade. Your till data can answer this: compare average spend per head on combo tables with non-combo tables at the same time of week.
Take the discount from the item with spare margin

Founders often discount the beer because it feels generous. Look at the numbers before you do. Your beer usually carries the stronger margin percentage, but the food carries the risk of waste. A dish made from prepped stock that will be thrown away tonight costs you almost nothing extra to sell. A pint that would otherwise stay in the tank until tomorrow still costs you its full margin if you discount it.

So build combos around dishes you want to move: items with high prep wastage, slow sellers that use the same base as popular dishes, or mid-afternoon plates that keep the kitchen busy. Keep the beer at or close to full price.

There is one exception. If a beer is near the end of its best condition, such as a hazy IPA four or five weeks in the bright tank with its hop aroma fading, a combo is a far better way to clear it than a discount on the board. Drinkers see a good deal on a meal, not a tired beer at a cut price.
Pair on flavour, not just on price

A combo is also a recommendation. Pair a crisp lager with fried pakoras or a wheat beer with a tandoori platter and guests trust the next suggestion too. A pairing that clashes, such as a heavy imperial stout with a delicate fish curry, feels like a sales trick.

Ask the brewer and the chef to choose together. The brewer knows which beer has the carbonation to cut through ghee and fried batter. The chef knows which dishes can carry a hop bitterness above 40 IBU without tasting harsh.

Three or four combos is plenty. Beyond that the menu gets cluttered, staff forget the rules and the till fills with modifiers nobody understands. Each combo should have a job: one to fill weekday afternoons, one to introduce a new beer, one to move a particular dish.

Put combos on a fixed time window if their job is to fill quiet hours. A combo offered at 9 pm on a Saturday competes with full-price orders you would have taken anyway.
Check the rules on alcohol promotions

Some Indian states restrict how alcohol can be promoted or discounted, including happy hours and bundled offers. Those rules change. Before printing a menu with beer bundled into a price, check the current excise rules for your state. Taxes on food and on alcohol are also charged differently, so ask your accountant how a combo should be split on the bill. Our note on running craft beer taps in Maharashtra shows how much state rules shape the menu.

Run a monthly report: combos sold, margin per combo and average spend per head on combo tables. Drop any combo that sells well but lowers spend per head. Keep the ones that lift it.

Building menu engineering like this into your routine is what separates a busy brewpub from a profitable one.

Your first step: take your best-selling combo and write down its margin against the same two items sold separately. If the gap is bigger than you expected, that is the combo to rework first.
faqs: Should a brewpub discount beer or food in a combo?
Usually the food, especially dishes with prep wastage or slow sales. The beer often carries the stronger margin and is easier to hold for tomorrow.
How many beer and food combos should a menu have?
Three or four, each with a clear job such as filling quiet hours or introducing a new beer.
How do I know a combo is working?
Compare average spend per head on combo tables with non-combo tables at the same times. If spend falls, the combo is giving margin away.
